speechtext:
I would like to take advantage of the presence of my hon. friend the Minister of Militia (Sir Edward Kemp) and also of my hon. friend, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane), to call attention to what I think is a very important matter, and to base a question upon it. I have before me a letter, part of which is as follows:
On January 17th, 1917, the St. John and other Canadian papers published with big headlines Mr. Guteltus' circular to employees of the Canadian Government Railway, asking for volunteers to operate trains in France, taking supplies and munitions to trenches. Among other conditions it stated: "And with the further understanding that they will receive wages made up of military pay supplemented by railway pay equal to' their present pay", etc. The required number were quickly secured, briefly drilled, sailed for England March 1st, and after delay of about a fortnight went to France, and of course are there now.
My information is that instead of the * promise made by Mr. Gutelius in his circular being carried out, these men are only receiving $34 per month, instead of in many cases $90 per month, which would be the amount of their railway pay. I think the ministers will agree with me that there is nothing more important than to keep faith with those who go to the front,
and nothing so calculated to interfere with recruiting as a failure to keep such a promise.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION TO APPLY RULE 17B CARRIED ON DIVISION.
MOTION TO APPLY RULE 17B CARRIED ON DIVISION.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I fear that under the baneful influence of the Government in office our institutions are becoming gradually Americanized, the use of the gavel in this House being a somewhat novel proceeding with us, but one which is common with our neighbours to the south of us. Whether the result will be a good thing for Canadian institutions or not I do not know, but certainly the introduction of this novel method of stopping debate accords well with the nefarious measure it is being applied to. We are here, Sir, dealing with the most serious question, as faT as the financial interests of Canada are concerned, that ha6 been before this Parliament for a long period of years. At an earlier period we heard a great deal about the tremendous obligations imposed upon this country by the Canadian Pacific Railway proposition. Although that proposition was a very great one, it is not comparable in the slightest degree, from the standpoint of the amount of the obligation which is being imposed upon the country, with this one which is being forced and crushed through this House without the slightest regard for the consequences. It is undoubted that the hon. the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) is induced to take this course because he has some facts to conceal, and be-

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: cause he is unwilling, or unable, to give to the Canadian people the information which they are entitled to receive before a measure having such tremendous consequences to the country passes through this House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the hon. member (Mr. Macdonald) accuses a minister of deliberately concealing facts and availing himself of the rules of the House for the purpose of so doing, he is going beyond the rules of debate.

I have a right to say that, as ah explanation of the reason why this closure is being applied, tjie Minister of Finance is unwilling to give the House the information that the House has a right to have.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Under our rules, the hon. member must take his seat. The second statement of the hon. member is not quite so objectionable as the former one, but still I think that both of his statements exceed the proper decorum of debate.

My second statement was an exact repetition of the first one. I have no desire to transgress the ordinary rules of debate but I have a right to say to the House and the country what I deem to be the correct explanation of why this measure is being forced through-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Yes; so long as the language of an hon. member is parliamentary.

I submit that my language is quite parliamentary in every particular. I was not suggesting motives. I was stating the reason why the Minister of Finance was using this novel method of forcing through this measure, and I have a right to do that.
We are discussing to-day the amendment proposed by my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) which declares that before this country is finally and positively saddled with this enormous liability of $650,000,000, together with whatever amount the arbitrators may choose to award for the stock which the Canadian people are supposed to get under this agreement, they should come back and submit to Parliament the question of whether or not that money should be paid. In view of the enormous liability, in view of the consequences which it will have for all time in the future upon this country from the financial point of view, such a reasonable proposition as that of my hon. friend from St. John ought to be accepted by this or any other government. When that proposition was made, what was the answer given by the right hon. the Prime
324i
Minister (Sir Robert Borden) last night? He told us that we should not think in this country of confiscating any person's property. Why did he not say so in 1914? When in 1914 he brought down the legislation by which he proposed to give the Canadian Northern Railway Company $45,000,000, he and his Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) said to the House and the country: Pass this legislation and we will have the right to confiscate. If it is wrong to-day it was wrong in 1914. The Solicitor General on that day, dealing with that measure, deliberately and solemnly announced to Parliament that the effect of it was that:
We now here bind you that should the day of default come you shall not appeal to the Parliament of Canada on the ground of your road being confiscated In any way whatever.
After that notice was given to Parliament in 1914 and the legislation was passed upon that understanding, what right has the Prime Minister to come to us to-day and tell us that we should hesitate about confiscation.
I have seen properties in which men have invested deliberately taken away, legislation passed in this House which was confiscation beyond all question, and when the Government pledged itself three years ago that it had the right to confiscate and could use that right and it would not cost the Canadian people five cents to get all the equity in this road, why should we have all these paltry excuses put forward to-day as reasons why they cannot confiscate when they have a right to? Then we hear that the Government had all the information necessary, that it had Mr. Bell's audit of the Canadian Northern accounts, that it had reports by Auditor Bell and reports of the Drayton-Acworth Commission and the report of Mr. Loomis. Why did not the members of this House have that information? Of what use is it to this Parliament, or to the people, if the Government have information which they decline to give out so that we may form a judgment? Let me give one or two illustrations of information so far withheld and without which this House is saddling this country with this enormous liability. The Finance Minister has not told Parliament, and apparently is not going to, the amount for which this stock is pledged with the pledgees, and this is information which the House has a right to receive. In addition to that, let me remind the Finance Minister that there are $25,000,000 of income convertible stock outstanding, and that at the time that stock, was issued and sold in Great Britain, aa

we are told it was, $25,000,000 of the common stock of the company was deposited with the National Trust Company as security, so that if the holders of the income stock desired common stock they could obtain it at any time up to the year 1919. That stock is in the hands of the National Trust Company. Has the minister told the House if any arrangement or understanding has been made with the holders of the income convertible stock in existence as to whether they will, before 1919, exercise their right to take that stock, which is now in the hands of the trustees?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That stock is not covered by this agreement at all.

Mr. Speaker, will
you take notice of any interruptions?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will give the ihon. gentleman full advantage of any interruptions,

Then we are told
with great gusto by hon. gentlemen opposite that they are getting absolute title to all the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway and of the subsidiary companies. And yet the Finance Minister, as you will find from Hansard of August 17, brought down a return in regard to certain subsidiary companies which showed that this Government and the Canadian people will not, as a result of this Bill, get all the stock of the subsidiary companies. There is outstanding $5,947,100 of that stock held by people outside, that being made up of $2,405,400 stock of the Canadian Northern Quebec Railway Company; $2,000 stock of the Central Ontario Railway Company; $2,940,000 of the Duluth, Winnipeg and Pacific Railway Company; $75,000 of the Halifax and Southwestern Railway Company; $500 of the Irondale, Bancroft and Ottawa Railway Company; $521,200 of the Quebec and Lake St. John Railway Company; and $3,000 of the Niagara, St. Catharines and Toronto Railway Company. That stock will not become the property of the Canadian people. But what will be the result? It will be that [DOT]unpaid dividends on stock guaranteed by the Canadian Northern in connection with the issue of debentures of these companies must be met. This stock is held by outside holders, and the result will be that some people, whose names are not known, whose names the Minister of Finance will not give to the House, will come into possession of stock which will be rendered valuable and be able to earn dividends, and in the case of debentures, receive their back dividends which have not been paid by the Canadian North-

ern Railway Company. Should we not know something about that amount. Is six million dollars approximately, so inordinately small a sum that nobody needs care about it? Surely in this time, when people are being taxed in every possible way, $6,000,000 cannot be disregarded. Yet hon. gentlemen are asking us to go it absolutely blind in regard to that matter, to pay no attention, whatever to it, and they give no information. Not only that, but all over this country there are coal companies, there are lumber companies, the stock of which has been held by the holders of the Canadian Northern railway stock. I venture to say that if you had >a correct statement of the stock pledged with the Canadian Bank of Commerce, it would be found that a large number of companies in which these gentlemen are personally interested have had their stock pledged by the holders with the Canadian Bank of Commerce, and that the argument will be *made to the arbitrators by the pledgees, whose indebtedness we do not know, that the value of the common stock of the Canadian Northern railway in the hands of Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann was very much greater by reason of the fact that it made valuable the stock in these coal and lumber companies a'll over the country, and on that account additional value should be given to the common stock of the Canadian Northern Railway, and it should be assessed at a higher rate. But we have no information with regard to it, the House and! the country are told to go it blind, to shoulder this liability, to assume all these charges. For what purpose? Not because of any proposition of Government ownership.. The Prime Minister last night talked fantastically about some system of co-operative management of railways, with glittering generalities, absolutely evading any statement of principle as to what the intention was, and the House is asked to accept *that beautiful reason as a justification of the assumption of this enormous liability, imperilling the financial position of this [DOT]country. I venture to predict that the Finance Minister, inside of six months, will be unable to sell the securities of Canada except at a figure so disgracefully low that every Canadian will hang his head in shame, and the cause of the' depreciation of our securities will be this infamous bargain which is being forced through the House to-day by the hon. gentleman. The Prime Minister tells us of all the information that the Government has yet, he is	carefully concealing it from

the House. I have indicated one or two items in regard to which we should have had information. I cannot, in the short time within which I am compelled to limit my remarks, deal with every one of these questions, but I have indicated some of them.
Then he told us what a terrible thing it would be for Canada if this enterprise was compelled to go into the hands of a receiver. Why, said the Prime Minister last night; you would have to appoint seven receivers; you would have to have seven courts at work and seven sets of lawyers; you would have conflicts as to earnings; you would have the road broken up into fragments, and seven different receiverships. I was astounded at the Prime Minister venturing to make that statement in the House. He is too good a lawyer, as I know from my association with him at the bar of my province, not to be aware that if he' was speaking from a legal standpoint and not from a political standpoint he would not have made that statement. Does he not know that, under the Exchequer Court Act of this country, it is open for this Government or for any creditor of the Canadian Northern Railway, in respect of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and each and every one of these companies which were mentioned in the schedule of the Act of 1914 as being railways declared to be for the general advantage of Canada- to go to the Exchequer Court and have one receiver appointed covering the control over every one of these railways. I make that statement and the right hon. gentleman cannot dispute it. I have the words of the Exchequer Court Act under my hand and I can quote them to the House to show that the judge of the Exchequer Court has power to appoint receivers whose power to deal with this question will be adequate and ample to cover the control of all of these railways.
The legislation of 1914 expressly declared that the subsidiary companies which up to that time had not been declared to be railways for the general advantage of Canada, should come under federal authority, and they were so placed, and they still are there. Therefore, why does the Prime Minister talk about seven receiverships, seven courts of law, and seven sets of lawyers, in the face of that fact when, so far as the interests of this country are concerned, through the judge of the Exchequer Court one receiver could be appointed, with all the ample powers which attach to a receiver, who could deal with this whole problem,
and during the time of stress and financial difficulty and uncertainty could keep that railway in operation and in such condition that we would be able to deal with it later on, when proper investigation wae had. But this is the reason, forsooth, why we cannot do anything except what the Government asks. Then my right hon. friend the Prime Minister told us they were following the Drayton-Aoworth report in three particulars. My right hon. friend should have told the House wherein he was not following the Drayton-Acworth report, and if he had done so, he would have found a good many instances other than the scanty three which he had to conjure up as some justification for his statement. There is not a line in the Drayton-Acworth report that recommends giving a cent of money to Maekenr zie and Mann. On the contrary they eay it is not "for value received," because there was no value in it. There might be a disposition made of a certain quantity of stock which should remain here, but no money w.as to be paid, and yet my right hon friend (Sir Robert Borden,) made an attempt to lead the country to believe that the Drayton-Acworth report recommended that Parliament should recognize the right of Mackenzie and Mann to be paid in cash. There is not a line of that report that warrants that statement, and it cannot be justified. Why my right hon. friend should have made that statement I am at a loss to understand, in view of the fact that the Drayton-Acworth report told us this stock was not worth a dollar, and not a dollar ehould be paid for it, yet Parliament is seriously asked to provide for an arbitration, and if the arbitrators are unanimous there is no appeal, and whether the arbitrators are unanimous or not we cannot in this Parliament exercise our discretion or our judgment in regard to it no matter what the state of-Canada may be financially six months from now. In other words, we, or our successors in this Parliament, will be tied hand and foot from this moment, and will be unable to do anything to relieve this country from the enormous liability that is being imposed on it. And, forsooth, the Finance Minister tells us about this professional arbitrator at Toronto, this wonderful gentlemen, Sir William Meredith, about whom no person could make any remark, who will be sure to give a verdict in favour of the Government. That was the position the Finance Minister took. Sir William Meredith either is earning his money as Chief Justice of Ontario, or he ia not earning it. I am glad to notice that

a Conservative senator has introduced a measure which I am told has been passed in the Senate, which provides that in the case of judges like Sir William Meredith, who receive very big fees, the amount of these fees shall be deducted from the salary which the country is expected to pay them. Either Chief Justice Meredith is performing his duty as Chief Justice of Ontario, or he is not. If he is performing his duty to the full he has no business going into matters of this kind; and, in view of the fact that he is the professional arbitrator of the Conservative Government of Ontario and of this Government, he is not an appointee to whom the country can give carte blanche and say: Take this question into consideration, and Parliament will never have the right to control it in any way. What the Prime Minister was attempting to talk about in regard to the co-operative management of these roads, I was unable to conceive last night, and after reading Hansard this morning I was unable to understand it. Was he telling us that hereafter the country was going to finance the whole three railways of the country? If that is the proposition we ought to know it, but the whole thing is in such a position of blissful uncertainty, with no information, that the country is being told to take it blind. Just one word, Mr. Speaker, before 1 close-as you are compelling me to close -in regard to this allegation that this House has had an opportunity to consider this matter. Let me give the dates. On August 2nd, the Minister of Finance made a statement about the railways. Then he said nothing for five days. On August 7th, he moved a resolution in regard to this matter, and the House went into committee on the 7th and 8th August. On the 9th August the first reading was given to the Bill pro forma. My hon. friend then sat down and said nothing. My time is up, but let me complete this sentence.

Sir WILFRID LAURIER: Mr. Speaker, it so happens that, on account of the circumstances in which the House is not interested, I could not be present during the greater part of the debate on this question, and this is the first opportunity I have had to intervene in it. As my time is limited, I cannot do more than touch on two or three of the points which are in issue. It is true that last evening my hon. friend the Finance Minister (Sir Thomas White) was kind enough to say that, so far as I was concerned, I might exceed the rules and take all the time I wanted. I am sorry to say to the Minister of Finance that I cannot even thank him for (this courtesy. It is recorded in the Great Book that King David and his companions were in the desert, suffering from thirst, and when some water was offered, the King, seeing that there was not enough for himself and his companions, would not touch it. I am in the same position today. There is not enough to go around the members of the Opposition, and I shall share with them the short ration of time allowed to each of us.
Therefore, I cannot do more than touch two or three points which were involved in this discussion, and the first to which I shall direct my attention will be to a statement made and repeated again and again from that side of the House by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), the first time he spoke, and repeated by my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) on more than one occasion-almost every time he was on his feet, and he was on his feet several times- and by my hon. friend the Minister of

Finance (Sir Thomas White) who declined to accept an invitation tendered him to go to the city of Toronto to discuss this question. The statement was made and repeated, that all the members on this side of the House, including myself and the member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) had agreed at one time to pay $30,000,000 for the stock of the Canadian Northern Railway.
Sir, let me tell the whole story, because the story as presented by hon. gentlemen opposite has been only partly told. In 1914,
I need not remind the House, the Canadian Northern was practically insolvent; at all events, it could not meet its liabilities or pay its fixed charges, and under such conditions, it was, by law, insolvent. It came to this House for assistance, and the question arose how Parliament should deal with it. Three courses were open to us then as now. The company might go into liquidation, it might be temporarily assisted, or the Government might take it over. We did not then, any more than we do now, favour this company going into liquidation, and in this Tespect our policy is different from that of the United States where many companies that have been in difficulties similar to those of the Canadian Northern have been allowed to go into liquidation. If I had more time at my disposal I should like to speak for a few moments on the difference in policy between the United States and ourselves in that regard, but I pass on. The Government decided at that time that we should assist the company. It was represented to us that if we advanced the sum of $45,000,000, that amount would enable the company to settle all their claims, meet all their liabilities, and complete the enterprise and make it a going and prosperous concern. The Government took every possible mortgage they could upon the assets of the company, and it is well in this connection for me to recite the Act to show the extent of the mortgage that was taken by the Government at that time securing the advance of $45,000,000, and the methods provided for the collection of it. First of all, let me say that the stock was increased from $77,000,000 to $100,000,000, by a stroke of the legislative pen, to use the graphic phrase of my hon. friend from Calgary the other day. The Government took $40,000,000 of the stock, and a mortgage upon the balance, and the company bound itself to grant " a first, fixed and specific mortgage or charge upon the shares " of the company. It also undertook to
(b) grant a specific mortgage or charge upon the mortgage securities and shares of stock now or from time to time hereafter deposited with and specifically mortgaged under the Trust Deed of the 30th day of June, 1903.
Cc) grant fixed, specific and floating mortgages or charges upon the undertaking of the Canadian Nortliern and its properties, assets, rents and revenues, and its rights, powers and franchises present and future.
Nothing was omitted. Everything that the company had in the way of property was covered by the mortgage. Then it was stipulated, and to this the company agreed, that in the event of default the mortgage would be foreclosed and everything would be lost by the company, even their equity of redemption. So far we made no opposition to the proposition made at that time by the Government. We agreed that we should take a complete mortgage upon everything that the company thad, and that in the event of default the company should lose everything it had mortgaged. That was tihe covenant; it is there in the law. Nothing could be more ample or more efficient than the mortgage we then took. But that proposition of the government provided one remedy, and one remedy only. It provided for the Government recouping itself for the assistance it had given to the company, in the event of default taking place. But we were not content with that on, this side of tihe House, because no provision was made whereby the Government could take over the road in the event of it proving a going and prosperous concern. The Government provided for our taking over the road in the event of default, in which case the company would lose everything it had, but the Government made no provision whatever for acquiring the property if the company was able to meet its liabilities and become a going and prosperous concern. That was the difference between the policy of the Government, and our policy.
My hon. friend from St. John moved an amendment that in the event of the company becoming prosperous we should make provision to acquire, not from an insolvent but from a solvent company, the property of the road for the benefit of the
4 p.m. Canadian people. His amendment contained four different provisions. The provisions were that the stock should not be $100,000,000, but should be reduced to $30,000,000; that this stock should be placed in tihe hands of the Receiver General to be held by him in trust for His Majesty for the period of five years; that if during that period of five years the company discharged its liabilities to the Government, made all the interest payments on the money advanced, and carried out all

So far as I am personally concerned, I have no feeling against Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, in fact I have nothing but admiration for the courage and ability they have shown in building this road. They have not only shown courage and ability, but I think they have, perhaps, built the road as cheaply as any person else could have built it under the circumstances. No doubt they were limited to a great extent as they went along by lack of capital, and we all know what that means to any one who embarks upon an undertaking of this kind. The Secretary of State told us the other evening, and several other hon. gentlemen have told us-I think the Prime Minister also made the statement-that if we took this road over under the scheme put forward by my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), it would mean confiscation. My right hon. leader has just spoken very clearly on that point, and has set forth my views, exactly. This canned possibly be conjured up as a case of confiscation. My hon. friend the present Secretary of State (Mr. Meighen)

said most explicitly and definitely, in 1914, that under no consideration were the owners of this road to come back for further assistance, and in the event of default they were not to raise the claim that we were confiscating their property. According to the Drayton-Acworth report, and according to Professor Swain's report, and taking over the liabilities of the road we are actually paying more than the road cost. Therefore, nobody can imagine we are confiscating the property. Altogether apart from that, the owners of the road made a bargain with us in 1914. They were notified then most clearly and definitely by the Solicitor General that if they failed in their enterprise and we took it over by foreclosure they must not, under any consideration, set up a claim that we were confiscating the road. Where two parties make an agreement, and one is not able to carry out his undertaking, if the other takes over the property under the agreement there is not, and there cannot be, any question of confiscation. If a man mortgages his property and fails to redeem it, if the mortgagee takes it over nobody ever dreams of confiscation. I have nothin** to say against the pledgees of this stock for doing the very best they can to get the highest price possible for the stock, and 1 have nothing to say against Mackenzie and Mann for doing the best they can to get the highest price possible for this stock. It is their right and their privilege as independent citizens to get all they can. At the same time, it is equally our right, as representatives of the people, to see that the interests of the country are guarded. My right hon. friend the Prime Minister waxed very indignant last night in regard to the resolution seconded by the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) in 1914, the effects of which resolution have just been stated 'by my right hon. leader, and stated that we were opposed to arbitration.
I have not heard any one on this side of the House express opposition to the principle of arbitration. What we claim is that in this case there is nothing to arbitrate. That is the position we have taken right along. The other day in committee the Government saw fit to vote through the proposition that the value of this stock shall be left to arbitration. That being so, it is our duty to see that the interests of the country are fully guarded by this arbitration. Both sides of the House have an equal responsibility in this, My hon. friend the member for St. John moved a very simple resolution, and one which will absolutely 
guard the interests of the people. It is to the effect that the finding of this arbitration board must be subject to the approval of the award by Parliament. Nothing can be more simple than that, and. in my judgment nothing can more completely safeguard the interests of the people. My right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) said last night that the reason they were taking over the stock instead of taking over the road itself was because they were leaving the operation of the road under its present management, or leaving the corporate entity absolutely as it was. We have been told by the Premier and also by the Minister of Finance that they were going to put this road in such a position that it would not be under the Governor in Council, and therefore would not be subject to party influence. They have not as yet given us any indication as to how the board of management will be organized, or how it will be appointed. If it is appointed by the Governor in Council it certainly must be under the control of the Governor in Council. and must be under party influence. There is only one way to avoid that and that is to appoint them in the same way as judges are appointed so that they are responsible to Parliament only. The people will never be satisfied with a commission to manage this road, or the roads of this country, unless it is in an independent commission and is composed of capable men. As to the personnel of the .board of arbitration, I have nothing to say against Sir William Meredith personally but I would have been very much more satisfied had some hard-headed, capable business man been appointed by the Government as their arbitrator. This is a business proposition after all. If we are going to arbitrate as to the value of this stock, the arbitration should be before hard-headed, capable, business men who have had experience and not before some judge who has been taken away from his business connections for a number of years. He may be absolutely fair in his mind and he may be capable but his business for years has had to do with proceedings in court. I have always been opposed to the appointment of judges on arbitration boards. Judges as a rule have been removed for years from intercourse with the business of the country. I have never been able to find out why judges are constantly appointed to arbitration boards because previous to their appointment the judges were probably only very ordinary so'icitors. There is no divine right by which they become more important after

they have got upon the bench than they were previously to going on the bench. For that reason I am opposed to that type of arbitrator.
I notice that the Minister of Finance has moved to strike out certain words and to omit certain clauses at the suggestion of the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) which I think improves the Bill in some ways. But, why he should strike out the words " on their own judgment " is something that I have not been able to realize.
I do not know whose judgment the commission will go by when they fix the amount of the award unless it is their own. They will hear evidence and all that sort of thing but why strike out the words " on their own judgment"? I do not know whose judgment they are going to leave it to, unless it is the judgment of the Governor in Council, or the Government, in that case, we should fix the amount now if there is going to be any amount. The .proper way would have been to have fixed the amount in this House if there was going to be any amount given.
I cannot understand why the Government, and especially the Minister of Finance and the Secretary of State, should continually harp on the question of our confiscating this property. It is absurd to talk about confiscating a property when we are really paying more than the property is worth by assuming the liabilities and at the time carrying out the agreement which was entered into only three years ago.
Last night the Prime Minister discussed something that he has discussed here once or twice before, and that is a co-operative management of the railways. That would mean the taking over of all the railways. While I have not given it serious enough, or long enough, thought to enable me to conclude whether I am in favour of government ownership of railways entirely or not, that would be the only way in my judgment by which individual, or co-operative, control could be brought about.
The right hon. gentleman referred to the operation of railways in England. That may or may not be successful from the financial standpoint. The railways in England are in a very peculiar position. They have certainly operated the railways in England from the war standpoint excellently since the war commenced, but they had the advantage of the advice of all the best managers of railways in England, who joined together for the purpose of operating them during the war. That could only be done in this country, in my judgment, by
the Government assuming control of all the railways and appointing one managing commission. If we are successful in the attempt to operate this railway, something of the kind may be brought about in the future.
But, in the meantime, we are not supposed to be discussing that; the only question is whether it is wise to adopt this simple amendment of my hon. friend from St. John which absolutely protects the interests of the people. The Prime Minister said last night: What do you think of a proposal to appoint arbitrators with a right of appeal to the Supreme Court and then an appeal to Parliament? I have always thought that Parliament was supreme, was the high court of this country. Therefore, I do not see any danger, or any farce, m forcing the arbitration board, or even the Supreme Court of this country, to submit their finding to the Parliament of Canada. Not the slightest injustice could be done to any person by Parliament. Otherwise, we are not fit for our positions.
I do not see anything in the suggestion of my right hon. friend that it would be absurd to allow an appeal from the arbitration board, and from the Supreme Court, to this Parliament. These are only ordinary individuals that we have appointed to these positions ourselves, or who have been appointed by the Government which represents the country. I have no doubt that my time has expired. I will urge in sitting down that the Finance Minister and the Government reconsider the position they have assumed on this matter. It is a very simple question. All we want is the absolute protection of the interests of the people, and that is all this amendment asks. Why the Government should not accept it without any hesitation is something that I cannot comprehend.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have risen immediately my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) sat down but I was not able to collect the references in time. I wish, with much respect, to say a few words in reply to his remarks, and also in reply to the remarks of my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt).
It is some time since I have heard the right hon. gent'eman endeavour to reconcile the various positions he takes on any question. That was a custom of his in earlier days, but lately he has given it up. I freely acknowledge that when he does so

undertake no one can excel him at the task. He delivered this afternoon a very skilful, and indeed very able, effort in endeavouring to show thaJt the position to which he commits his party to-day is not exactly the opposite of that to which he committed the same party three years ago. The line he takes is this, he says: Three years ago you introduced legislation providing for the event of default; a bankrupt company approached Parliament and said: We cannot proceed without the assistance of this House; Parliament acquiesced in the request, and provided for only one event, provided for the event of default in later days on the part of the company, and provided that should such default take place, then we could foreclose the equity of redemption and it should become our property. He then went on to argue that we did not provide for the event of success, and that the purpose of his amendment to the third reading of the Bill at that time was to take care of that contingency and to see to it that, should the road succeed as a result of the assistance given, Parliament should have the right to take the property as the property of the people and to go in for Government ownership of a successful road. I wish first to aver that both his positions are incorrect. His statement is not a correct statement of what Parliament provided in the event of default, and his statement that the policy of the Opposition was to cover the contingency of success is likewise incorrect. We did provide for the event of default, and the provision for the event of default was not that, should default come, the equity of redemption should be, without conditions, foreclosed. Why did the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) leave out the whole terms of section 24? We provided thaJt if default should come Parliament should fix the terms and conditions, if any, upon which the equity of redemption should be valued. Now what is the meaning of "fix terms and conditions" if, under no circumstances, terms and conditions were to be fixed? The leader of the Opposition said they were satisfied with that clause. Now will you tell me what was the meaning of Parliament saying that terms and conditions would be fixed if, under no circumstances, terms and conditions should be fixed? He was satisfied with the clause, virtually assuming that there could be circumstances following default under which it would be proper to fix terms and conditions. Now,
I ask, under what circumstances could it be proper to fix terms and conditions following default, if not under the very cir-
j cumstances of to-day? We have been through three years of war. The difficulties the company is in to-day are difficulties that arose very largely from the war. I do not suppose their earnings have diminished by reason of the war, except that it has been impossible for them to complete their line owing to financial difficulties, and they have so not been able to get their full earnings. They have not been able to link up with Montreal or to get money out of securities which we have guaranteed. They have fallen short by many millions of dollars. Abnormal conditions have arisen so that the position today is surely exactly the condition upon which terms and conditions should be fixed and under which drastic measures should not be adopted, if there could be conditions in which drastic measures should be adopted. It is true there might be conditions under which we should fix those conditions. Those were referred to by the Prime Minister in one of his earlier addresses, namely where it was admitted that there was no equity of redemption to be valued, and, in the latter part of my right hon. friend's address, he himself admitted that if there was a real, substantial equity of redemption there, he himself would not confiscate it even now. Therefore it becomes a question: is there a real equity of redemption or is there not?
I said a moment ago that the leader of the Opposition was wrong as well when he intimated to Parliament that the purpose of his amendment to the Third Beading of the legislation of 1914 was to provide for the contingency of the road succeeding, to enable Parliament and the country to take over and operate a road that was successful in the hands of a private company. The right hon. leader of the Opposition was careful. It took him some days to think this reconciliation out. He was careful to read his amendment, and he was careful to read clause 24, but he was not so careful to read his own speech of that date. If he will read his speech he will find that the purpose of his amendment was not to provide for the road succeeding at all, but to provide another method of government ownership should the road fail. He laid down in his speech in the most explicit terms that for a successful road he would have nothing to do with government ownership. He was against it if a private company could succeed with the road. He wanted government ownership only if they had to keep coming back to Parliament for

further assistance. At page 4634 of the Hansard of 1914 the right hon. gentleman said:
But I have nothing to disclaim of what I said on that occasion.
That is on some previous occasion when he opposed government ownership.
Or upon any other occasion-that I never was favourable to the operation of railways by the Government. I do not say that there are not some countries more settled than we are in which this might not be a good policy. I did not say that this was a policy which might not be a good one in a country that is much more settled than ours; but in a new country such as this I thought that operation by company was preferable to operation by Government. Such was my view. I expressed it with perfect frankness and honesty to Parliament and the country at that time. With reference to the Transcontinental railway, in a country such as this, as between government operation and company operation, I favoured operation by a company.
Then later on he said:
I am not enamoured any more of government ownership than before, but if we have to make a choice to-day, and if the choice we have to make is between pouring more money into the coffers of the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the Government getting control of the road, I would rather get control of the road for the benefit and profit of the people of Canada. That is the view that I have to present to the House on the present occasion.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
So that he was not providing at all for the contingency of success, he was providing for the contingency of failure, and he said: If we have to keep on pouring more money into the road, let us not do it, but if a private company can succeed with it I am in favour of a private company keeping it, and not the Government of Canada. He was even more explicit on a previous day when he said:
If we could have had some assurance that this is the last call, and that they will not come back knocking at our doors again, there might he some reason to treat t.hem as they request.
That is the way the Bill was.
But we cannot have any such assurance. On the contrary, I think it is a matter of absolute certainty that, in view of the figures placed before us, in view of the undertaking ' which they have to carry out and of the conditions, they cannot complete that enterprise with the assistance of the $45,000,000 that is to he voted by this Parliament.
A matter of absolute certainty; he foresaw the failure of the road, and its coming back to Parliament again.
Therefore, he says, some new position has to be taken, and he proceeds ic argue what the position should be. He refers to the
previous amendment moved by the hon member for St. John and he said that amendment had two features; first to reduce the stock, and second to provide for taking over the road. He said the first was of no importance, and he put it aside, and he dealt with the provision for taking over the road, because, as he said, with the $45,000,000 assistance, in his judgment it was an absolute certainty the company would come back again. How is it then that he can argue to-day that in 1914 he had in mind the successful operation of the road, and1 that such was the contingency he was providing for by his amendment. It was the very opposite he was providing for, as expressed by his own words. He says again:	I never, while I was in power, as
Premier of Canada, confiscated the property of any man. I would not do so to-day. But he tells us that we are taking the property which has liabilities to the extent of $30,000,000 greater than its assets. Upon what can this Parliament assume, on any* principle of equity or honour, that that road which we are taking over has $30,000,000 of liabilities more than its assets. Did he ever while he was Prime Minister of Canada take the ex parte report of a commission, before whom the other party was never heard to determine the valuation of property this country expropriated? He never did. He provided for the Trancontinental railway. He expropriated property all the way [DOT] between coast and coast; he expropriated the property of Mackenzie and Mann, on the flats of the city of Winnipeg, amounting to almost $1,000,000, He did not provide in that case that, if Parliament was not satisfied with the determination of the courts of the land, the Supreme Court, being the final arbiter, Parliament should review and override, and act as a court of appeal over the Supreme Court. He never expropriated the property of any one while he was Prime Minister, unless on the report of a judicial tribunal, before whom the interested parties could be heard. Why does he now suggest doing the contrary? Why does he assume that, because the Drayton-Acworth report came to a conclusion without hearing the other party at all-a purely ex parte report-there was not surplus of assets over liabilities, and consequently that Parliament should assume there was not. If there is no surplus of assets over liabilities, we will have nothing to pay. All we ask Parliament to declare is that a properly constituted tribunal shall try the case, and if we are taking the property with $30,-

000,000 more liabilities than assets, that tribunal will so find. We are only asking Parliament to establish a tribunal before whom the parties can be heard, and the tribunal will determine whether or not the stock which we are taking, which represents the equity of redemption, has or has not a real substantial value. If it has no value they will so find, and if it has a value they will fix it. The ultimate tribunal under the Bill is the same as the ultimate tribunal under the Expropriation Act; it is the Supreme Court of Canada.
We have confidence in the tribunal to which we are going to appeal, and we will be bound by the decision of that tribunal. Referring to the remarks of the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt): It is true that the Parliament of Canada is the high court of the nation,but the functions of the Parliament of Canada are not judicial functions, they are legislative. When judicial functions are to be exercised, we establish tribunals and delegate to them judicial functions. We do so by this Bill, and we utilize the Supreme Court of this country, which is the ultimate tribunal in judicial dispute. If any wrong principle has been adopted, if anything is cited as a fact which is against the weight of evidence, it all comes before the Supreme Court of Canada, and they exercise their judgment in appeal oveT the tribunal of just such men as the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) thinks are best qualified to establish values. Now, then, where is the reason in this case to establish Parliament as a court of appeal over the Supreme Court, that did not exist in every other case of expropriation that we have ever heard of? If we are to make Parliament a court of appeal over the Supreme Court in this case, why do we not do it in proceedings under the Expropriation Act? Why not do it under every Act under which we expropriate? Why discriminate in this case? Is there any more reason to distrust the arbitrators and the Supreme Court of Canada, which reviews their findings, in the present case than in any other case? Why should they be deemed incompetent? Why should they be corrupt here, if they are not corrupt in other cases? Why should Parliament presume to assume judicial functions here, when they do not presume to assume such functions in any other case that has ever come before them.

It appears to me that the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Meighen), who has just finished replying to the hon. leader

of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), has taken the most extraordinary ground. We have seen a good many political somersaults turned in one way or another, but surely the Secretary of State does not think he can cover up his own somersault, in the case of the Canadian Northern Bill now before the House and the Canadian Northern legislation of 1914, by simply saying in an offhand way that he has seen the leader of the Opposition try to justify himself many times, but never so unsuccessfully as to-day. Let me quote his own words. He said: It is some time since the hon. leader of the Opposition attempted to justify his various positions.
Well, surely, even from the Secretary of State's own argument, the leader of the Opposition has not taken any more positions on the Canadian Northern railway question than have the Secretary of State (Mr. Meighen) and the hon. Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White). And may I add here, in parenthesis, the last part of the argument of the Secretary of State implies that he has practically no [DOT] faith in the commission appointed to make the Drayton-Acworth report. He asks: Is it right, or would anybody think of taking the obiter dictum of two or three men who are appointed, without having the right to go to some higher place, to have it confirmed or otherwise? .
If the Secretary of State says that to-day I ask him: did he at the time, or did the Government at the time they appointed that commission, have faith that the Government would act on the report of the Drayton-Acworth Commission? If they did, why not take that course? If they did not, why does the Government not tell us candidly that the Drayton-Acworth-Smith Commission started out on a fishing expedition, to see what they could find, and that the Government was going to consider their attitude after the commission reported. The Secretary of State makes a strong argument in his own mind, and refers to section 24 of the Act of 1914, which says:
If authorized by the Parliament of Canada the Governor In Council may, on such terms and conditions as Parliament may prescribe,-
And then he goes on to argue that the terms and conditions to-day are extraordinary in regard to the taking over of this road by the Government. I think the House and the country will agree with me that the terms and conditions of the taking over of this road at the present time are most extraordinary-extraordinary in view

of the legislation of 1914, which expressly provided in section 24 that, if further default were made, the Government would have the right to take over that equity of redemption by foreclosure, and close the whole transaction, and thus the people of the country would become the owners of that road.
The Secretary of State and the Minister of Finance tell us that it would not be right for the Government to take over the road without paying the company for the equity of redemption. How in Heaven's name they can say that, when their own commissioners have told them that the liabilities against the road are greater than its assets, I do not know. Where is the equity of redemption? There is nothing there to arbitrate about, absolutely nothing.
The whole trend1 of section 24 leads us to one conclusion, and one conclusion only, and that is that the understanding in 1914 between Mackenzie and Mann and the Government was this:	Mackenzie and Mann
said1: " Give us $45,000,000. Throw around the advance whatever safeguards you like, we don't care how drastic they may be. This $45,000,000 will tide us over and put us on our feet. We shall never have to come back to Parliament for assistance again, and consequently we will enter into this hard and fast bargain; that if we do come back to Parliament for assistance you may, willy nilly, take over the road under section 24." That was the understanding when the legislation was passed in 1914. The Finance Minister said in his heart at that time:	" Here we are at the end of this
long Canadian Northern haul. We will make no two bites at a cherry, but will give them $45,000,000 now, and if they ever come back again we will off with their heads without a word." The Finance Minister gave credit for the framing of that Act to the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) who was its father. The Finance Minister, speaking of that Act, said:
TVhat security have we? I have seen a good deal of financing in my time, and I know something- of law although my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) does not think so, and I want to say this:	I have never seen as
effectual a means of entering into possession of a property upon which a mortgage is held as has been devised by the Solicitor General in connection with this transaction.
The Act was the Solicitor General's haby, and he was proud of it then.

speechtext: He repudiates his child to-day.

To-day he wishes it had
another parent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You are not going to "take off my hat."

No, that paragraph has been quoted so often that the minister will be completely bald if his hat is taken off any more. You can't get away from the fact that that statement of the Minister of Finance was to be read into section 24, and he thereby said: "The Government through its able Solicitor General has so surrounded this agreement with safeguards that in case of default the people of this country, if they desire, can take over the road without the payment of another single coppeT." Again, in 1914, the Minister of Finance said:
I was dealing with the question of remedy upon default, and was pointing out that we have a much better control than would be afforded by the security of a majority or all the stock of the Canadian Northern.
He was again, referring to section 24, the section upon which the Government was going to act. If at no other time, the minister, in those very words, which appear in Hansard, notified Mackenzie and Mann then and there that that was the intention of the Government. I submit that when a contract has- been entered into in good faith betwen two parties and when neither party will be prejudiced 'by the carrying out of the -contract, after full notice has been given and under conditions which make chicanery absolutely impossible, there is only one thing to do-more especially in this ease where the contract is not between private individuals, for the Government are acting for the people of the whole Dominion of Canada and have no right to change the terms of the contract entered into between the people and Mackenzie and Mann -and that is to carry out the contract.
To my mind there is no justification whatever for this Bill. I am always willing to do the fair thing. I am always willing to see money paid by a private individual or by a government for money's worth. But when somebody tells me that in this case we are confiscating property in which Mackenzie and Mann have an equity of redemption, in view of the fact that the Government's commissioners have said that the liabilities against the road are greater than its assets, I want somebody to tell me where this mythical equity of redemption is and why the people of Canada should pay a single dollar for it.
Besides -all that, I believe the people of this country think that Mackenzie and Mann have done moderately well out of

the Dominion of Canada and its 5 p.m. component parts. Gather into one big pail what Mackenzie and Mann have milked from our different municipalities, counties, and provinces, and from the Dominion as a whole, and I do not think there is a man in this House who would not say that Mackenzie and Mann have received from the people of Canada everything to which they are entitled. They have not been able to make the road a success. That is unfortunate for them, 'but it is not our fault; and they have no right, simply because interested persons desire this Government to do certain things in regard to the stock, to ask this Parliament to pay for stock that. is absolutely worthless.
In conclusion, I wish to say a few words as to the Government passing this measure by applying the closure. Outside of the war this is perhaps the biggest question which the people of Canada have ever had to consider. A question involving the assuming of liabilities to the amount of $600,000,000 will surely stand all the light of day and all the consideration hon. members of this House can give it. This measure, until closure was applied, had been under discussion for about eight days only, and I say eight days is none too much for this House to consider a transaction involving an increase in our national debt to an amount never dreamed of by any person in this country. The Secretary of State, discussing the amendment of the hon. member for St. John, asks whether the right hon. leader of the Opposition had ever asked Parliament to ratify the purchase of a property involving an expenditure of $1,000,000 in Winnipeg, or some other amount somewhere else. I ask you, Sir, whether this transaction involving hundreds of millions of dollars is on an equal footing with million-dollar transactions that took place under the right hon. leader of the Opposition? It is a horse of entirely different colour. You cannot treat the two things alike.
Perhaps the principle is the same, but the principle is absolutely swallowed up in the enormous sum of money for which the people of Canada will become liable in this case. Therefore, I say that, so far as foreclosure is concerned, the Government seem to be.in an extraordinarily great hurry to rush the measure through this House without having given all the information which we on this side desire, and to put it upon the statute book before the light of day has been properly turned upon it.

I want to avail myself of this last opportunity in OTder to protest strenuously against this unfair measure which a moribund Government are endeavouring to force upon the people of this country.
I will say further that their attitude is not based upon -any fair or reasonable ground, and had we not been used for six years to this regime always prone to offend common sense, we would have much more cause to wonder now.
The discussion raised by the Bill submitted by the Government has thrown a new light upon certain clear, plain and concrete facts, wnich have served as a justification for the strenuous opposition of lion, members, from this side of the House and have enabled us to understand the resentment of the people in presence of the sad exhibition the Government are making of themselves. In fact, it is hardly conceivable that such a measure as we are now debating could have been laid before this Parliament.
This measure is invidious and iniquitous. Indeed what does the Government proposal amount to? It is intended to acquire the stock of the Canadian Northern now in the hands of holders so that the country may own this stock and in order to have those shares valued, to make out the amount the Canadian people shall be called upon to pay to Mackenzie and Mann and their confederates, it is intended to appoint arbitrators -who' shall determine without appeal the amount we shall have to put up in this transaction. Upon their *award, without any interference from, this Parliament, the present Government shall pay unscrupulously, unhesitatingly out of the public treasury to a few favourites of this regime a sum amounting to $60,000,000 in their estimation.
The members on this side of the House recriminated. They shall protest to the last. They say to fhe Governmeht: You have the unquestionable right to get hold of this stock, to lay your hands upon that railway and the holders cannot claim a cent. Consequently, it is useless to appoint arbitrators for making the valuation of the stock, and when we consider that in this transaction we are assuming an indebtedness of $400,000,000, evidently the contention of the Government that, in so doing, they would unjustly confiscate private property, is an absurd contention -which is not. worth considering.
Mr. Speaker, our proposal is unassailable. We are confronted by a contract which

clearly provides under section 24 that .should the Canadian. Northern make default in paying the interest on the sums then granted by this Government-and nobody would deny that that contingency has materialized long .ago. and that the company has actually defaulted-the Government would be ipso facto, entitled to get hold of that stock and to lay their .hande upon that railway, without any special process of law and without being bound to pay .a cent to .anybody for this stock.
Section 22 of that Act throws still .more vivid light upon the intentions of the Government and shows that they intended to provide against that default on the part of the company, by pointing out the meane the Government .should resort to in order to operate the railway in case the contingencies anticipated by article 24 came to pass.
To-day, Mr. Speaker, the anticipations of the Government in 1914 have materialized. The 'Canadian Northern company have defaulted and relying upon that statute, we say to the Government: do not thus throw away $60,000,000 of the people's money; do not be so generous with the funds of others so as to favour a few millionaires from Toronto.
We are not alone to take that position. The opposition to this, measure is not confined to the opponents of the Government.
We have seen influential financiers of the city of Montreal most strongly protesting against this Government proposal. We have had the opportunity of reading their protest which has been published by several newpapers of this country. These gentlemen are friends of the Government. But before being partisans, they are enlightened and well informed citizens who before all wish to save the country from the hands of those who seem intent, cost what it will, to push it into ruin and bankruptcy. These gentlemen have read this Act of 1914, .and to .add to this rather conclusive evidence, they remembered the Drayton-Acworth report which states that the Canadian, Northern stock has. no actual value. Nevertheless, and in spite of all that, the Government w.ho>
preach economy to the people without ever practising it themselves, dare throw this 1914 Act to the wastebasket and, in order to again favour Messrs. Mann et al who have by their millions put the hon. gentlemen, into power, conceive the odious design of saddling once more the people- and that, without any necessity-with a
new burden of $60,000,000. Mr. Speaker, in times of peace .such a, policy would have been a blunder, but in war times, it is a crime.
>Do we realize, Mr. .Speaker, what that transaction is going to cost to the country? The member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) lias given us fabulous figures, almost incredible figures. This railroad acquisition will cost us $650,000,000, and our national debt, with this amount .added to it, now reaches a total of. $2,250,000,000. The meaning and the scope of these figures may be better understood, when we recall the fact that this war is costing us presently almost $1,000,000 per day.
Do you not think, Mr. Speaker, that the people of this country are now sufficiently taxed by the ever-increasing expenses of the war without adding to them this new burden? Why not follow the system, adopted by the United States .and put the Canadian Northern in the hands of a receiver? That policy has been a .success in the United States, w.hy should it not succeed in Canada? Whatever be the case, let us consider the fact that, for the past three years, this Government has stated before this House and before the country, that our only preoccupation should be to win the war. The people have not recriminated; they have borne the tax without a murmur, even though the indirect tax is being increased .and the direct tax imposed. The Government are preaching economy to the people, should they not set the example, should they not practise what they preach unto others? Do they pretend that, by taking $650,000,000 to buy a. railroad they will thereby make our participation to the war more effective? Our national credit, Mr. Speaker, is affected by this legislation.
Quite recently we borrowed in the United States the sum of $100,000,000 and. we .had to pay over 8 per cent interest on that amount. Our credit, therefore, is not what it used to be. If we mean to take an active and really efficient participation in this war, we must above all keep our credit in good .shape. Please tell me, Mr. Speaker, when this proposal shall be known abroad, .in all its details, when our bankers shall .have weighed and analyzed what the Government are doing and intend to do, will they he very anxious to lend more money to this Government, and if they do so, what kind of a rate will they demand?
